title: liquidGL
lede: A framework-free JavaScript library by NaughtyDuk that renders refracting glass panes over live web content with WebGPU or WebGL.
summary: WebGPU and WebGL glass panes with refraction, bevels, and specular light for the web. 2025–2026.
made: 2025 (repository created June 21, 2025; still maintained in October 2026)

evidence.note: Inspected the repository file assets/images/_0006_multiple-lenses.jpg (2400 × 1260) in a scratchpad copy. The repository also holds frost-and-specular and menu-bar images, which were downloaded but not reviewed. Not stored.

styles.note: The most complete web version of the material: refraction, bevel, specular light, and tint. Its demos use glass for content tiles, which goes beyond Apple’s rules.

context: The README: liquidGL “turns any fixed or sticky-positioned element into a perfectly refracted, glossy ‘glass pane’ rendered in WebGPU (with automatic fallback to WebGL)”, and “recreates Apple’s ‘Liquid Glass’ aesthetic in the browser”. It falls back to CSS backdrop-filter and offers tint, chromatic aberration, and stacked lenses. [GitHub](https://github.com/naughtyduk/liquidGL).

The LICENSE file is MIT, “Copyright (c) NaughtyDuk”. Wikipedia calls it the most actively maintained of the widely used web implementations as of September 2026. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A photo of a red running track with the legs of runners and their shadows.

Six rounded glass tiles form a fitness dashboard: distance, heart rate (a large “137 BPM”), speed, power, resistance, and an interval delta. Labels are small uppercase white sans-serif with green accents.
Each tile has a bevelled rim where the track texture and the white lane line bend and magnify. The line through the heart-rate tile kinks at the tile edge.
Rims catch thin highlights, and the tiles keep the red-brown color of the track. A large white “liquidGL” wordmark sits at the lower right.
interpretation: The library shows that the refraction can be reproduced on the web, but only with a shader and an offscreen copy of the page, not with CSS alone.
borrow: Concentrate the distortion in a narrow bevel and keep the center of the pane flat, so text inside stays readable.

rights.statement: The code is MIT (© NaughtyDuk). Kept as link only because the demo image shows a third-party photograph whose license is not stated.
